Will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric blanket? (US 120 V)

Yes, it runs it — no usable-capacity figure see why below ↓

Every check passes: 60 W running against 1,800 W continuous. Nothing here has a locked rotor to publish an inrush figure for, so the absence of one is a fact about the hardware rather than a hole in the library.

Official spec + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-01 · US 120 V unit × electric blanket

Nominal capacity 1,024 Wh
Surge headroom 10×+

Two numbers decide this, and readers arrive using them interchangeably. Watts are the ceiling on what the inverter can hold at any instant — an electric blanket needs 60 W of them while it runs. Watt-hours are how much energy the battery holds, and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus holds 1,024 Wh of them on the nameplate. A machine can have plenty of one and not enough of the other.

The verdict above is a calculation — running watts, start-up inrush and inverter waveform against this machine's continuous output and surge ceiling — not a lookup. What it will not do is print a runtime, and the reason is specific: we read 2 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-01 and found no depth of discharge or inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them, so there is no usable-capacity figure to divide.

Where those numbers come from

Every figure below carries the tier it came from and the date it was checked. A blank is never left blank: a field we have found no figure for says so, and a field whose sources disagree — two documents, or one document with itself — says that instead of picking one.

No usable-capacity figure for this machine

EcoFlow states a nameplate watt-hour number for it, and we read 2 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-01 and found no depth of discharge or inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them. Dividing the nameplate by this load would be wrong by 20–35% in the flattering direction, so this page shows the nameplate for what it is and refuses to turn it into hours.

Missing: station.usable_capacity_wh

Energy rate instead of a runtime

60 Wh per hour averaged over this load’s duty cycle

This number needs no battery figure at all, which is why this page can give it when it cannot give hours. Divide any usable-capacity figure you trust by it and you have your own runtime, with our arithmetic visible instead of hidden.

Questions people ask about this pairing

Will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric blanket?
Yes. 60 W of running draw against 1,800 W of continuous output — 3.3% of it. The verdict is computed from running watts, start-up inrush and inverter waveform — the working is in the evidence section above.
How long will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric blanket?
We will not put a number on it, and that is a finding rather than a gap. We read 2 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-01 and found no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them. What it does state is a nameplate watt-hour rating. Dividing that nameplate by this load produces a figure that is typically 20–35% too high while looking exactly as authoritative as a real one. What this page gives instead is the load's energy rate in watt-hours per hour, which needs no battery figure at all.
Why is there no runtime on a page that says yes?
Because "yes it runs it" and "yes for this long" are two different claims with two different evidence requirements, and this machine only supports the first. The verdict needs a continuous rating and a surge ceiling, which EcoFlow publishes. Hours need a usable-capacity figure, which it does not. Twenty of the twenty-six machines in our library are in that position, and the alternative — nameplate watt-hours divided by label watts — is the single most common wrong number on this topic.
